_comment: Best Practices reference, fully data-driven. Each section renders as an accordion panel with a Do list (green) and Don't list (red), plus one example scenario. Reviewed and approved by ERM subject-matter experts as of lastReviewedByERM. Set a section's "draft" back to true if it needs re-review (shows a Draft tag until cleared).

sections.title: Appropriate Uses of AI
dos: Use AI to draft, brainstorm, summarize, and reorganize non-sensitive material.
Use it to get unstuck — outlines, first drafts, alternative phrasings.
Treat AI output as a starting point that you review and revise.
Prefer University-provided tools (U-M GPT, U-M Maizey) for work tasks.
donts: Don't use AI as the final authority on facts, policy, or legal questions.
Don't paste confidential, regulated, or personal data into tools not approved for it.
Don't use AI for decisions that require human accountability without human review.
Don't assume output is accurate just because it sounds confident.
sections.example: A staff member uses U-M GPT to draft a first version of an internal FAQ, then fact-checks and edits it before sharing — appropriate. Using it to generate a final compliance determination with no review would not be.

sections.title: When Human Review Is Required
dos: Require human review for anything external-facing, high-impact, or decision-critical.
Have a knowledgeable person verify facts, figures, names, and citations.
Document who reviewed AI-assisted output and when.
Escalate anything touching legal, HR, financial, or regulated matters.
donts: Don't send AI-generated content to leadership or external parties unreviewed.
Don't rely on AI for final numbers, deadlines, or commitments without checking.
Don't skip review because the output 'looks professional.'
Don't treat AI as a reviewer of its own work.
sections.example: Before a summary of a risk assessment goes to a dean, a subject-matter expert reviews it for accuracy and completeness. High-impact and external-facing output always gets a human check.

sections.title: Protecting Confidential Information
dos: Know your data's classification before using any AI tool with it.
Use only tools approved for that data classification.
Strip or anonymize identifiers when the task allows it.
When in doubt, leave sensitive details out of the prompt.
donts: Don't paste personal, health, financial, or otherwise regulated data into unapproved tools.
Don't upload documents you don't have the right to share with a third party.
Don't assume 'private mode' means the data is protected.
Don't include credentials, keys, or passwords in prompts.
sections.example: Instead of pasting a spreadsheet of names and IDs to get a summary, a staff member summarizes the aggregate patterns without the identifying columns.

sections.title: Citation Practices
dos: Disclose when AI meaningfully assisted in producing content, per local norms.
Cite the original, authoritative source — not the AI tool — for facts.
Verify that any citations an AI provides actually exist and say what's claimed.
Follow applicable style, disclosure, and academic-integrity guidance.
donts: Don't present AI-generated text as independently researched when it wasn't.
Don't trust AI-provided citations without checking them — they are often fabricated.
Don't cite the AI tool as a primary source for factual claims.
Don't omit disclosure where transparency is expected.
sections.example: An AI draft references a policy 'Section 4.2.' The author confirms that section exists and says what's claimed before citing it — and cites the policy document, not the AI.

sections.title: Fact-Checking Procedures
dos: Independently verify every factual claim, statistic, name, and date.
Cross-check against authoritative primary sources.
Be extra skeptical of specific numbers and quotations.
Build verification time into any AI-assisted workflow.
donts: Don't publish or forward unverified AI claims.
Don't accept a source just because the AI named it.
Don't assume recent events are covered accurately.
Don't let time pressure replace verification.
sections.example: Before including a statistic from an AI summary in a report, the author traces it to the original dataset and confirms the figure and its context.

sections.title: Avoiding AI Hallucinations
dos: Ground the tool in your own trusted sources when possible (e.g., U-M Maizey).
Ask the tool to indicate uncertainty or cite where a claim came from.
Prefer summarizing text you provide over asking for facts from memory.
Treat confident, specific-sounding detail as a prompt to verify, not to trust.
donts: Don't ask an AI for facts it has no reliable way to know.
Don't assume grounding eliminates errors — still verify.
Don't use fabricated-looking quotes, cases, or references.
Don't equate fluency with accuracy.
sections.example: Rather than asking 'what does U-M policy say about X,' a staff member pastes the relevant policy text and asks the tool to summarize it — grounding the answer in the real source.

sections.title: Writing Quality Standards
dos: Edit AI drafts for accuracy, tone, and your own voice.
Ensure clarity, correct terminology, and appropriate reading level.
Keep formatting accessible (headings, plain language, alt text).
Make sure the final product reflects your judgment, not just the tool's.
donts: Don't ship AI text verbatim without editing.
Don't let AI introduce jargon, filler, or an off-brand tone.
Don't sacrifice accessibility for stylistic flourish.
Don't lose the specific context the AI couldn't know.
sections.example: An AI-drafted announcement is edited down for plain language, correct unit names, and an accessible heading structure before it's sent.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
dos: Consider fairness, bias, and who could be affected by the output.
Be transparent about AI use where people would reasonably expect it.
Respect privacy, consent, and intellectual-property rights.
Keep human accountability for decisions that affect people.
donts: Don't use AI to make consequential decisions about people without oversight.
Don't ignore signs of biased or unfair output.
Don't misrepresent AI-generated content as human-authored where that matters.
Don't offload responsibility onto the tool.
sections.example: When AI is used to help screen or summarize information about individuals, a person remains accountable for the outcome and checks for biased or unfair patterns.
